reason: The pointwise limit is identified explicitly, and the fixed choice \(\varepsilon=1/2\) supplies a valid witness against the uniform convergence criterion for every index threshold.
text:
For each \(x\in[0,1)\), \(x^n\to0\), whereas \(f_n(1)=1\) for every \(n\). Hence \((f_n)\) converges pointwise to
\[
f(x)=\begin{cases}0,&0\le x<1,\\1,&x=1.\end{cases}
\]
If \((f_n)\) converged uniformly, its uniform limit would necessarily equal this pointwise limit. Fix \(\varepsilon=\tfrac12\). For every \(N\in\mathbb Z_+\), take \(n=N\) and \(x=2^{-1/N}\). Then \(x\in[0,1)\), so \(f(x)=0\), and
\[
|f_n(x)-f(x)|=x^N=\frac12.
\]
Thus, for every \(N\), there exist \(n\ge N\) and \(x\in[0,1]\) such that \(|f_n(x)-f(x)|\ge\varepsilon\), which is precisely the negation of uniform convergence to \(f\). Therefore \((f_n)\) does not converge uniformly on \([0,1]\).
